title: All is opinion
hook: everything is opinion, and opinion is in your power (Meditations 12.22)

segments.voice: Yesterday: two gates, one for acts and one for words. Your line was if not true, don't. Did a small fib stop at the gate? Day six hundred thirty-three.

A text arrives: "we need to talk." Nothing else. In the next four minutes, the mind can get you fired, dumped, and blamed for something you can't remember doing. Then the follow-up lands: "about the weekend plans." Notice what happened. The words didn't change. The world didn't change. What changed was the story built around four words. For Marcus Aurelius, that gap, between what happens and what we make of it, is where much of our trouble lives. And it's the one place we can reach. Today: all is opinion.
screen: `"WE NEED TO TALK."` → `"ABOUT THE WEEKEND PLANS."` → `THE STORY CHANGED, NOT THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Way back in book two, Marcus had written himself a short line. In George Long's translation: "Remember that all is opinion." Now, in book twelve, he comes back to it. In 12.22 he says, more or less: take your opinion away whenever you choose, and like a sailor who has rounded the headland, you'll find calm water, everything still, a bay without waves. First, what opinion means here. The Greek word is hypolēpsis: an assumption, the judgment you add to a thing. Not the event, but the label. "This is a disaster." "She did that on purpose." Second, what Marcus doesn't mean. He isn't saying nothing is real, or that facts are just viewpoints. The text came. The weekend plans exist. What's opinion is the weight: harmful, insulting, ruined. Third, the part that makes it practical: the opinion is yours. Events aren't in your power. Your reading of them is, at least a little, at least after a breath. That's why it's the hopeful half of the teaching. If the storm were out there, you'd have to wait for the weather. If much of it is in here, you can row toward the bay. Fourth, a neighbor. Marcus links the idea in book two to a Cynic named Monimus, who apparently said that everything is smoke, or vanity. Marcus takes the sharper edge off it: not that nothing matters, but that what we add to things can be taken away. It's a move he practices again and again in the notebook.
screen: `HYPOLĒPSIS: THE LABEL WE ADD.` · `NOT "NOTHING IS REAL."` · `THE OPINION IS YOURS TO CHANGE.` · `ROUND THE HEADLAND, FIND THE BAY.` · then, large: `IN MY POWER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring up one thing that's bothering you right now, small or big. Say plainly, in your head, what actually happened, as if you were a camera: who said what, what arrived, what's on the calendar. Then notice the label you've stuck on it: unfair, a disaster, typical. Now try, on purpose, a different label that's just as honest: inconvenient, unclear, not finished yet. Don't force a feeling. Just hold the new opinion beside the old one and see what the water does. The bell holds the time.
All is opinion. Marcus's reminder that what weighs on us is mostly the judgment we add to events, and that judgment is ours to take away. Today's word.
Your line: in my power. The next time a message or a moment knots your stomach today, separate the camera's version from your label, and choose the label again. Day six hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often practice separating what happened from the judgment they've added to it, describing the event plainly and then choosing how to read it.

original.note: Greek: an assumption, a judgment or opinion. Marcus's word in "all is opinion."

trapdoor: what you thought: all is opinion means nothing is really true.
what it means: the event happens; the label we add to it is ours, and can be taken away.
what a scholar hears: hypolēpsis, a key word in Marcus, tied in 2.15 to a saying of the Cynic Monimus, and returned to in 12.22 with the image of a sailor rounding a headland into calm water.

notes: Confirm Long 1862's wording of 2.15: 'Remember that all is opinion.'
12.22 paraphrased (take away opinion when you choose; the sailor who has doubled the promontory finds calm, a waveless bay). Confirm the image.
Confirm ὑπόληψις is the Greek word in 2.15 (πάντα ὑπόληψις) and in 12.22.
Monimus's saying is reported as calling everything typhos (smoke, vanity, delusion). Hedged with 'apparently'; confirm.

Editor review (year 2): fixed two counts ("we need to talk" is four words, not three; Long's "Remember that all is opinion" is not four words), softened "almost all of our trouble" and the "taking-up" etymology of hypolēpsis, and toned down the hook's telling the listener what they'd imagine.
